did_you_know.text: This chapter presents the prophecy of Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
Isaiah calls heaven and earth as witnesses and compares Israel to children whom the Lord raised and honored, yet who rebelled against him.
The prophet uses a striking comparison: even an ox and a donkey know their owners, but Israel does not know the Lord or understand.
Daughter Zion is portrayed as lonely and vulnerable—as a shelter in a vineyard, a hut in a cucumber field, and a besieged city—after the land’s devastation.
Isaiah emphasizes that only a small remnant survived, and because of it Judah did not become like Sodom and Gomorrah.
The Lord is not satisfied with an abundance of sacrifices; the chapter teaches that religious worship without moral reform is unacceptable to him.
The call to repentance involves not only stopping evil but also washing and cleansing oneself—that is, making a real change in one’s conduct.
The practical path to reform is to learn to do good, seek justice, defend the orphan, and plead the widow’s case—in other words, to protect the vulnerable in society.
The Lord offers the possibility of forgiveness and change: sins as red as scarlet or crimson can become white as snow and wool.

Jerusalem is described as a city that was once faithful and full of justice but became a city of murderers, bribery, and neglect of orphans and widows; later, its purification and the restoration of justice and righteousness are promised.
